knownFor: A teacher of Latin rhetoric from Africa who was at Nicomedia when the Great Persecution began in 303. He answered it with the Divine Institutes, a handbook of the true religion argued to educated pagans from their own poets and philosophers, which holds that religion cannot be forced. On the Deaths of the Persecutors, which most scholars hold his, tells how the persecuting emperors died. Jerome says that late in life he taught Constantine's son Crispus in Gaul.
datesNote: No birth year and no death year is held. Jerome says he was summoned to Nicomedia in Diocletian's reign; Paul Monceaux reckons he arrived about 290, at about forty. He was teaching in Bithynia when the church at Nicomedia fell, on the day the editors convert to February 23, 303. Schanz holds that he had left Bithynia by 305 or 306, and Monceaux that he left in late 305 or 306. Monceaux says he conceived the Divine Institutes about the start of the persecution and wrote them between early 307 and early 311, and puts On the Deaths of the Persecutors about 314. Jerome places the teaching of Crispus in his extreme old age; Crispus was made Caesar on March 1, 317, and Monceaux puts the teaching about 316, Schanz about 317. William Fletcher's notice says he is believed to have died at Trier (Treves) about 325; Monceaux says nothing at all is known of his last years or the date of his death
placeNote: From Africa, by Jerome, who calls him a pupil of Arnobius and says he wrote a Banquet as a young man in Africa and an Itinerary, in hexameters, of a journey from Africa to Nicomedia; Nicomedia in Bithynia, the Greek-speaking city that Diocletian made his eastern capital, where he taught Latin rhetoric; Gaul, where Jerome says he taught Crispus. Monceaux holds that he was almost surely born in Africa, probably in the region of Cirta and Mascula; William Fletcher reports an older view that he came from Firmum on the Adriatic, which Monceaux rejects. Jerome says only Gaul, not Trier
role: Teacher of Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia; Christian writer in Latin

keyWorks.title: Divine Institutes
keyWorks.about: seven books, a handbook of the true religion argued to educated pagans: the gods who were once men, the philosophers who contradict one another, true wisdom and religion, justice, true worship, and the happy life and the end of the world after six thousand years and a thousand-year reign. Book V says religion cannot be forced and must be defended by dying, not by killing. In it he says he trained young men in oratory not to virtue but to cunning wickedness, that he was never eloquent because he never engaged in public speaking, and that he saw in Bithynia a governor elated because one Christian who had held out for two years seemed at last to yield. He says Tertullian was obscure and Cyprian answered a pagan with Scripture the pagan thought false, and that a newcomer must be refuted by his own authorities. Some copies open with an address to Constantine

keyWorks.title: On the Deaths of the Persecutors
keyWorks.about: addressed to Donatus, who had been tortured nine times and was freed from a jail where he had lain six years. It tells the fall of the church at Nicomedia, the edict, the palace fires, the man who tore the edict down and was burned alive, Galerius's disease and the edict of 311, the edict of Milan posted at Nicomedia, Constantine's dream before the battle at Rome, and the deaths of the emperors who persecuted, ending with the killing of their families, among them a boy of eight and a girl of seven. It counts ten years and about four months from the overthrow of the church to its restoration. It survives in one manuscript, and the Library holds it in English only, in Lord Hailes' translation

keyWorks.title: On the Workmanship of God
keyWorks.about: a short book on the making of man, addressed to Demetrianus, which Jerome calls On the work of God or the creation of man. It opens by saying how disturbed he is and in the greatest necessities. Monceaux dates it to the last months of 305, a little before the Divine Institutes, and reads its opening as the cry of a man who had just lost his school, which is his inference

traces: Augustine says Lactantius used the Sibylline testimonies, bringing them in bit by bit as his argument needed them, and that he himself set them down in one connected series in the City of God.

His book on the persecutors keeps the edict of Milan: A. C. McGiffert notes that the greater part of the edict is extant in its original Latin in chapter 48 of Lactantius's book, and that the Greek translation in Eusebius's Church History is still less accurate.

Paul Monceaux says the pamphlet rests on the most exact and complete account we have of those years, and that coins confirm many facts that Lactantius alone reports; he also calls it very partisan, with every persecutor a bad prince and every one punished.

Monceaux says he is rarely named in early Christian writing and only from the end of the fourth century, that his direct influence on his own time seems almost nil, and that he was widely read in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.
Calvin ends one argument with Lactantius, that no religion is genuine that is not in accordance with truth, and tells readers to read Lactantius and Eusebius on images.
remembered: Jerome says Lactantius has a flow of eloquence worthy of Tully, meaning Cicero, and wishes he had been as ready to teach Christian doctrines as to pull down those of others.

Jerome charges that Lactantius, in his books and particularly in his letters to Demetrian, altogether denies the subsistence of the Holy Spirit, yet asks who can forbid him to read the Institutes, in which Lactantius wrote against the Gentiles with much ability.
Jerome's Chronicle calls him the most eloquent man of his time and says he was so poor in this life that he often lacked even the necessities.
Jerome counts him among those who held that after the resurrection the Lord would reign in the flesh with the saints.
A list later credited to Pope Gelasius sets the little works of Lactantius among the books not received; whether Gelasius wrote the list is disputed.

uncertain: His life is Jerome's, and Jerome wrote some seventy to eighty years after the events: the Chronicle about 380 and the Lives of Illustrious Men in 392. The books are his own. No single witness carries the whole life. Jerome says he was summoned to Nicomedia in Diocletian's reign and names no one who summoned him; Lactantius himself writes only that he was called thither.

Where he was born. Jerome has him from Africa. Monceaux holds it almost sure that he was born there, but this is his reconstruction. Fletcher reports an older view that he came from Firmum, which Monceaux rejects.

His name. Jerome gives Firmianus, known also as Lactantius. Monceaux reads the full name, L. Caecilius Firmianus who is also Lactantius, from two African inscriptions and takes the second name for a nickname. The one manuscript of On the Deaths of the Persecutors names its author L. Cecilius.

When he became a Christian. Schanz says it is not known whether in Africa or at Nicomedia. Monceaux holds it almost sure that it was at Nicomedia, between 290 and 303, and says he was certainly a Christian in February 303, since he tells that he grieved to hear pagans attack Christianity. Fletcher guessed a link between his poverty and his conversion; Coxe's note says he sees no force in the suggestion.

Whether he saw the church fall. The account of its fall is in On the Deaths of the Persecutors. In the Divine Institutes he says only that he was teaching in Bithynia at the time the temple of God was overthrown. Monceaux writes that he saw the church destroyed there and the first edict posted.

Who wrote On the Deaths of the Persecutors. The one manuscript names the author L. Cecilius, and Jerome lists a book of Lactantius On persecution. Monceaux, after weighing the dispute, judges the case for his authorship more likely and says scholars lean more and more that way; Schanz lists it as Jerome's De persecutione, whose authenticity he says is disputed. Most scholars hold it his, and some have doubted it.

The cause of the palace fire at Nicomedia. Lactantius says Galerius's agents set it. Eusebius says only that a fire broke out in the palace, he knows not how, and that it was laid by a false suspicion on the Christians. Constantine, years later in the speech Eusebius preserves, says lightning destroyed the palace and the emperor's chamber, and that eyewitnesses, he among them, declare it. McGiffert, an editor, thinks the case against the Christians pretty strong and links the lightning to this fire.

The address to Constantine. Some copies of the Divine Institutes open with an address to Constantine. Samuel Brandt, in 1890, set the addresses aside as later additions; Monceaux, in 1905, calls them a forger's work; Schanz, in 1922, reports that Brandt later gave up that view and holds them Lactantius's own, from a second edition. Whether Lactantius wrote them is disputed.

The two writers he answers. The philosopher who preached poverty and dined well, and who wrote three books against the Christians, is unnamed in the Divine Institutes; Brandt's apparatus says the name is unknown and notes that Baronius thought Porphyry was meant, which Holstenius refuted. The judge who urged the persecution and wrote two books to the Christians is not named there either. The editors identify him with Hierocles, whom On the Deaths of the Persecutors names as the author and adviser of the persecution; that identification is the editors' and Monceaux's.
When he taught Crispus. Monceaux puts it about 316, with Crispus about sixteen; Schanz says he was called to Gaul about 317, with Crispus born about 307. Both place it late, after 315.

How and when he died is not known. Fletcher's Trier or Treves, about 325, is an editor's belief. The death in 325 printed with Jerome's notice in the English translation is the translation editor's note, not Jerome's. The name the Christian Cicero is a later editors' name, not an ancient title.

Judgments that belong to editors and later writers, not to Lactantius. McGiffert thinks the man who tore down the edict deserved death; Monceaux sketches Lactantius as a timid Christian without a calling to martyrdom. Each is that writer's own view.

briefReferences: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 12, tr. Lord Hailes: the church at Nicomedia, forced open at first light, its Scriptures burned, its furnishings pillaged, within view of the palace; Diocletian fearing the city would burn; the Pretorian Guards with axes leveling it in a few hours. Divine Institutes V.2, tr. William Fletcher: he was teaching rhetorical learning in Bithynia, having been called thither, when the temple of God was overthrown.

Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80: summoned to Nicomedia in Diocletian's reign, taught rhetoric there and turned to writing for lack of pupils, it being a Greek city; in extreme old age tutor in Gaul to Crispus Caesar, son of Constantine. Jerome, Chronicle, and Brandt's Latin of the same entry: the teaching of Crispus.

On the Deaths of the Persecutors 13, 14 and 15: the edict of the next day that stripped Christians of honors and dignities and subjected them to tortures; the palace fire laid to Galerius's agents; the presbyters led to execution, people burned in crowds, and servants cast into the sea with millstones about their necks. Eusebius, Church History VIII: a fire in the palace at Nicomedia, he knows not how. Constantine, Oration to the Assembly of the Saints, as Eusebius gives it: lightning, with eyewitnesses.

Divine Institutes V.2 and V.4: the two men who insulted the truth as it lay overthrown, a philosopher and a judge, and why Lactantius took up the task. Divine Institutes V.1 and V.4: Tertullian obscure, Cyprian answering Demetrianus with Scripture, and the newcomer fed milk and refuted by his own authorities.

Divine Institutes, Books I to VII: the gods who were once men, the sibyls, the philosophers who disagree, true wisdom and religion, true worship, and the six thousand years. Divine Institutes V.19 and V.20: religion cannot be imposed by force, and is to be defended by dying, not by killing.

On the Deaths of the Persecutors 33 to 35, 42 and 48: Galerius's disease and his edict letting Christians be Christians again, posted at Nicomedia on April 30, 311 (the editor's date); the edict of Milan posted at Nicomedia in June 313.

On the Deaths of the Persecutors, opening and last chapters: addressed to Donatus, tortured nine times; written so that all who shall arise hereafter may learn; the families killed, among them a boy of eight and a girl of seven, and the verdict that the wicked received according to their deeds. Dating and authorship: Monceaux, Schanz, and the single manuscript.

Jerome, Letter 58 and Letter 84: Lactantius's eloquence and the wish that he had taught doctrine as readily as he pulled down others; the charge on the Holy Spirit, and the question who can forbid reading the Institutes. Augustine, City of God XVIII.23: the Sibylline testimonies set down in one connected series.

A. C. McGiffert, notes to Eusebius, Church History: the edict of Milan extant in its original Latin in chapter 48 of Lactantius's book. Paul Monceaux, Histoire littéraire de l'Afrique chrétienne III: the book as the most exact account of the period, and very partisan.

quotationOriginals.modern: Spurred on by their proud ungodliness, by my awareness of the truth itself, and, as I believe, by God, I took up this task.
quotationOriginals.printed: being incited both by the arrogant impiety of these, and by the consciousness of truth itself, and (as I think) by God, I have undertaken this office
quotationOriginals.original: et illorum superba inpietate stimulatus et ueritatis ipsius conscientia et, ut ego arbitror, deo, suscepi hoc munus
quotationOriginals.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.4, English tr. William Fletcher, Latin ed. Samuel Brandt
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Brandt's Latin, not Fletcher's English. The brief ends the quotation at this task; Lactantius's sentence goes on, in Fletcher's English, that with all the strength of my mind I might refute the accusers of righteousness. Fletcher's arrogant impiety of these is the brief's proud ungodliness (superba inpietate), and his this office is the brief's this task (munus). Brandt's apparatus reports that earlier editors thought a word was lost after deo; the printed text reads as quoted. A second scan of Brandt's edition reads the same Latin apart from scan faults.

quotationOriginals.modern: Religion must be defended not by killing but by dying, not by cruelty but by patient endurance, not by crime but by faithfulness.
quotationOriginals.printed: For religion is to be defended, not by putting to death, but by dying; not by cruelty, but by patient endurance; not by guilt, but by good faith
quotationOriginals.original: defendenda enim religio est non occidendo sed moriendo, non saeuitia sed patientia, non scelere sed fide
quotationOriginals.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.19 (chapter 20 in the English edition), English tr. William Fletcher, Latin ed. Samuel Brandt
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Brandt's Latin, not Fletcher's English. Fletcher's putting to death is the brief's killing (occidendo), his guilt and good faith are the brief's crime (scelere) and faithfulness (fide). A second scan of Brandt's edition reads the same Latin.

quotationOriginals.modern: He was the most eloquent man of his time, but so poor in this life that he often lacked even the necessities.
quotationOriginals.printed: uir omnium suo tempore eloquentissimus, sed adeo in hac uita pauper, ut plerumque etiam necessariis indiguerit
quotationOriginals.work: Jerome, Chronicle, the entry for the year Crispus was made Caesar, as Prosper copies it in Brandt's collection of ancient witnesses to Lactantius (Latin)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: No English translation of the Chronicle is held, so the brief renders the Latin. The printed wording is Prosper's copy of Jerome's entry, which leaves out Latinis litteris (taught Crispus in Latin letters) before the quoted words; the words quoted are the same as in Jerome's own entry in Fotheringham's edition (lines 44984-44986 of that file), where a margin number and the word olymp stand beside the last line and eloquentissimus breaks at the line end. Brandt's collection also prints Jerome's own entry (lines 11241-11243) with the same words and a stray letter before tempore.
